newsitem.title: CANADA: FOCUS-Canadian real estate stocks return to favor.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Canadian real estate stocks return to favor.

text.p: Canadian real estate stocks have regained investor favor after languishing for years following the industry's collapse earlier this decade.
The rebound has been fueled by Canadian interest rates at 40-year lows, a pickup in the economy and good prospects for long-term growth, analysts said.
"The real estate sector is on the rebound, not only in a fundamental sense, but also in a stock market sense," said Frank Mayer, real estate analyst with HSBC James Capel Canada.
"It has forced people to realize that there's life after death."
Evidence abounds of the rebirth of real estate.

The real estate sub-index of the Toronto Stock Exchange hit a two-year high this week, powered by such companies as TrizecHahn Corp, Intrawest Corp and Cambridge Shopping Centres Ltd. The sub-index has soared more than 40 percent since early September.
Real estate investment trusts (REITs) have also performed well and the real estate stock rally has prompted a wave of new equity issues.
The rebound of real estate stocks contrasts sharply with the sector's performance a few years ago, when collapsing real estate prices and rental fees hit many high-profile developers.

Besides the collapse of the Reichmann family's closely held Olympia & York Developments Ltd, Canadian companies such as Bramalea Ltd and Trizec Corp were forced into bankruptcy or restructurings by the early 1990s recession.
For analysts who witnessed the demise of many Canadian real estate companies, the resurgence of the sector is a welcome change.

"The survivors in the industry feel like people who have emerged from a prolonged period in the desert. It's a nice feeling after what they've been through," said Rossa O'Reilly, real estate analyst with CIBC Wood Gundy Securities Inc.
Low interest rates were the biggest factor in the resurgence of real estate stocks, analysts said.

The Bank of Canada has lowered rates sharply since May 1995, bringing prime lending rates at Canadian banks to 40-year lows. The lower borrowing costs have translated into big savings for many Canadian real estate companies.

"There's an enormous one-time only opportunity for the industry to refinance its debt at substantially lower levels," said Jim Doak, managing director of equities with brokerage ScotiaMcLeod. "The cost of financing is the major cost in the industry."

Analysts said the drop in interest rates also meant that the rate of return on many properties, such as office buildings and malls, was now well above the cost of financing. Investors were therefore willing to pay more for many real estate companies and REITs.

Another positive for real estate stocks is a bright outlook for the Canadian economy, believed to be set for prolonged expansion amid low interest rates and inflation. This positive outlook has led many investors to view real estate companies as a good long-term buy.

"I'm looking for a long-term cycle here. I'm looking for four or five years of pretty solid growth in both the economy and the real estate industry. So there's a very favorable outlook," said Harry Rannala, a real estate analyst with Research Capital Corp.
